title: The Mongol World
tagline: Follow Genghis Khan's empire from the steppe to the rival khanates and Timur's heirs.
intro: In 1206 a kurultai on the Mongolian steppe proclaimed Temüjin Genghis Khan, and his armies built the largest contiguous land empire in history. Within two generations his sons and grandsons ruled from Sarai on the Volga, from Persia and Iraq, from the Silk Road cities of Central Asia and from Dadu in China, and the succession war of 1260–1264 split the empire into khanates. This path follows each of them: the Golden Horde and the Rus' princes, the Ilkhanate that ended the Abbasid Caliphate, the Chagatai realm that produced Timur, and Kublai's Yuan Dynasty, closing with the Timurid Empire, whose courts at Samarkand and Herat lasted until 1507.

steps.why: The oldest surviving work of Mongolian literature tells of Temüjin's youth and his struggles with the Tatars and Merkits before his rise to power.
Proclaimed Genghis Khan at a kurultai in 1206, Temüjin built the largest contiguous land empire in history, which split into rival khanates after 1260.
A grandson of Genghis Khan, Batu led the western campaign of 1236 to 1242 into Rus', Poland and Hungary, then ruled the western steppe from Sarai.
From Sarai on the Volga, Jochi's descendants took tribute from the Rus' princes for over two centuries, until the Great Stand on the Ugra in 1480 ended Moscow's tribute.
Another grandson led the Mongol campaigns into south-western Asia in the 1250s, sacking Baghdad in 1258 and ending the Abbasid Caliphate.
Hulagu's khanate in Persia and Iraq became a Persianised Islamic state under Ghazan, who converted in 1295 and began sweeping reforms with Rashid al-Din.
Genghis Khan allotted Central Asia's steppe and Silk Road cities to his son Chagatai; the khanate turned Muslim and Turkic and lost Transoxiana to Timur by 1370.
Great Khan and founder of the Yuan Dynasty, Kublai completed the conquest of the Song in 1279, and his disputed succession helped break the empire apart.
Ruling China from Dadu, the Yuan linked it to Persia and Europe across the Mongol network until floods, inflation and the Red Turbans brought it down in 1368.
Timur, produced by the Chagatai realm, conquered from Anatolia to the borders of China, and his heirs made Samarkand and Herat centres of painting, poetry and astronomy.

title: Japan from Jōmon to Meiji
tagline: Follow the Japanese archipelago from its first potters to the emperor's restored rule.
intro: For some 14,000 years the people of the Japanese archipelago lived mainly by hunting, gathering and fishing, and their potters made the world's oldest known ceramics. Wet-rice farming came with the Yayoi, and the Yamato court around Nara extended its authority over much of the islands. From the late twelfth century warrior governments held power: the Kamakura and Ashikaga shogunates, then, after the unification begun by Oda Nobunaga, the Tokugawa shoguns at Edo. This path follows that story to 1868, when the Meiji Restoration returned power to the emperor and set Japan on the way to becoming an industrial great power.

steps.why: For some 14,000 years hunters, gatherers and fishers lived in settled villages here, and their potters made the world's oldest known ceramics, around 14,500 BCE.
Farming migrants from the Korean Peninsula and the continent brought wet-rice farming, bronze and iron, and mixed with the Jōmon population from about 300 BCE.
Centred around modern Nara, the court from which the imperial line descends built keyhole-shaped burial mounds and received writing and Buddhism through Baekje.
Founded by Emperor Kanmu in 794 on a grid modelled on Chang'an, the capital on the site of modern Kyoto remained the imperial seat for more than a thousand years.
Victor over the Taira in the Genpei War of 1180–1185, Yoritomo set up a warrior government at Kamakura and received the title of shogun in 1192.
Turning against the Kamakura shogunate in 1333, Takauji took Kyoto in 1336 and in 1338 became shogun, founding the Ashikaga, or Muromachi, shogunate.
A warlord of the Sengoku period, Nobunaga began the military unification of Japan that Toyotomi Hideyoshi continued and Tokugawa Ieyasu completed.
After victory at Sekigahara the Tokugawa shoguns ruled from Edo, keeping some 260 daimyo in check through two and a half centuries of internal peace.
Perry's expedition and the unequal treaties undermined the shogunate; in 1868 Emperor Meiji declared power restored, and the domains and the samurai class were abolished.
Born of the Restoration, Japan went from feudal isolation to industrial great power in barely a generation, until a war it could not sustain ended in surrender in 1945.

title: Korea through the Ages
tagline: Follow the Korean Peninsula from its early farming villages to its division in 1945.
intro: Archaeologists name a long stretch of Korean prehistory after the plain pottery of the Mumun farmers, whose villages gave way to the first chiefdom-like societies in Korea. Gojoseon fell to the Han in 108 BCE, and the Three Kingdoms of Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla contended for the peninsula until Silla, allied with Tang China, destroyed its rivals and then expelled the Tang. Goryeo reunified the peninsula in 936 and gave Korea its Western name; Joseon, its longest-ruling dynasty, made Neo-Confucianism the basis of the state and created the Korean alphabet. The path ends with the Japanese protectorate of 1905 and the division of 1945, which left two Korean states.

steps.why: Named after its plain pottery, the culture of c. 1500–300 BCE saw intensive farming, large villages and the first chiefdom-like societies in Korea.
The last king of Wiman Joseon, the final phase of Gojoseon, refused to submit to Emperor Wu of Han, whose invasion took his capital in 108 BCE.
The largest of the Three Kingdoms ruled Manchuria and the northern peninsula, and its fortresses held off Sui and Tang invasions for seventy years.
The south-western kingdom, known for refined Buddhist art, passed Chinese writing, Buddhism and craftsmen to Yamato Japan before falling to Silla and the Tang in 660.
Allied with Tang China, Silla destroyed Baekje and Goguryeo, expelled the Tang by 676 and presided over a Buddhist golden age at Gyeongju.
Founded by Wang Geon in 918, the dynasty that gave Korea its Western name carved the Tripitaka Koreana and endured Mongol overlordship from 1259.
Korea's longest-ruling dynasty, founded by Yi Seong-gye in 1392, made Neo-Confucianism the basis of state and society and survived Japanese and Manchu invasions.
Created in 1443 under King Sejong and promulgated as 'the proper sounds for instructing the people', the alphabet became Korea's national script in the 20th century.
Pushed through with troops around the palace after the Russo-Japanese War, the treaty made Korea a Japanese protectorate; Japan annexed the country in 1910.
Split at the 38th parallel in 1945, the peninsula gained two rival states in 1948, and the armistice of 1953 left it divided along the Demilitarized Zone.

title: Kingdoms of Southeast Asia
tagline: Follow the trading ports, temple cities and sultanates of mainland and island Southeast Asia.
intro: Funan, generally considered the first known kingdom of Southeast Asia, traded through its port of Óc Eo with India, China and the Roman world. Along the Mekong, the Vietnamese coast and the straits, later states drew their wealth from sea trade, rice and tribute, and built in stone: the Sailendras raised Borobudur in Java, the Khmer kings Angkor Wat, and the kings of Pagan some 10,000 Buddhist monuments on the Irrawaddy. This path follows these kingdoms in the order of their rise, closing with Ayutthaya on the Chao Phraya and the Muslim sultanate of Malacca, which the Portuguese took in 1511.

steps.why: Generally considered the first known kingdom of Southeast Asia, Funan traded through its port of Óc Eo, where Roman gold medallions and Indian and Persian goods were found.
A confederation of Cham principalities on the coast of present-day Vietnam, whose fleets controlled the spice and silk trade of the South China Sea from the 7th to the 10th century.
The Khmer principalities that broke from Funan absorbed it under Isanavarman I, before Jayavarman II proclaimed the Khmer Empire in 802.
From Palembang in Sumatra this sea power ruled the Strait of Malacca, taxed China-India shipping and became a renowned centre of Buddhist learning.
One of the largest Buddhist monuments in the world, the temple was built in central Java under the Sailendra dynasty, closely connected to Srivijaya.
Founded in 802, the empire ruled much of mainland Southeast Asia from Angkor, where vast reservoirs and canals paid for Angkor Wat and Angkor Thom.
The first state to unite the Irrawaddy valley built some 10,000 Buddhist monuments on the plain of Bagan before Mongol invasions in the 1280s broke it apart.
The high point of Hindu-Buddhist Java claimed suzerainty over much of the archipelago, its fleets paid for by Brantas rice and the spice trade.
The Siamese kingdom on the Chao Phraya absorbed Sukhothai in 1438 and welcomed Chinese, Japanese, Persian and European merchants until Burma destroyed it in 1767.
Founded about 1400 by Parameswara under Ming protection, the port became the great entrepôt of the strait and a centre of Islamic learning until the Portuguese took it in 1511.
